title: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
summary: How a nested loss puts the most useful information first in an embedding, so a prefix of the vector works as a smaller embedding, and how to use that for cheaper storage and shortlist-then-rerank search.
outcomes: Explain why the first m numbers of a normally trained embedding are a poor small embedding
Truncate and re-normalize a vector, and show why skipping re-normalization can reorder results
Compute the summed Matryoshka loss over prefix sizes and explain MRL-E weight tying
Compute storage per vector and per index for any number of dims and precision
Design and cost a shortlist-then-rerank or funnel search on one Matryoshka vector

lessons.title: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails

blocks.md:
Recall from semantic search: an encoder turns each text into one unit-length vector, and search ranks documents by cosine similarity to the query vector. Every downstream cost of that vector grows with its length $d$. Storing $N$ vectors takes $N \times d$ numbers, and an exact search compares the query with every stored vector, about $d \times N$ multiply-adds per query.

The Matryoshka paper (Kusupati et al., NeurIPS 2022) points out that at web scale this *use* of the vector costs more than computing it. Yet a model hands out one fixed size, say 768 or 2048 numbers, whether the task needs that much or not.

Before Matryoshka, there were three ways to get a smaller vector:

1. **Train a separate model per size.** The paper calls these fixed-feature (FF) models. Accurate, but you train, store and run one model per size, and every size needs its own copy of the encoded corpus.
2. **Compress after training**, for example with SVD (keep the top principal directions) or a random projection.
3. **Just keep the first $m$ numbers** of the big vector and throw the rest away. Free, and it needs no second model.

blocks.prompt: Option 3 costs nothing. Take a ResNet50 trained normally with a 2048-number output and keep only its first 8 numbers for nearest-neighbor classification on ImageNet-1K. A separately trained 8-number model gets 58.9% accuracy. What do you expect from the chopped vector?
blocks.reveal:
About **2.4%**. The paper measured this baseline (Table 2, 1-NN accuracy): the first 8 dimensions of the 2048-d model score 2.36%, against 58.93% for a model trained at 8 dimensions.

A normally trained network has no reason to put important information first. The paper notes that deep models tend to *diffuse* information across the whole vector, so any 8 coordinates are a thin random slice of it.

scenes.caption: m = 2048: all three are the same full vector, about 71.2% (numbers from the MRL paper, Table 2, ResNet50).
m = 256: the chopped vector already trails the separately trained model (65.75 vs 69.72). SVD holds up well here.
m = 64: chopping loses 20 points. SVD still works, but it needs a projection fitted on the full corpus.
m = 16: chopping is nearly useless (12.06). SVD falls to 46.02. Only the dedicated small model stays high.
m = 8: 58.93 for the dedicated model, 2.36 for chopping, 19.14 for SVD. Small sizes need a model trained for them.

blocks.md:
So we face a choice between paying for many models (option 1) or losing accuracy at small sizes (options 2 and 3). **Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)** removes the choice. It trains *one* model so that the first $m$ numbers of its vector are, by themselves, a good embedding for several sizes $m$. Like nested Russian dolls, each small vector sits inside the bigger one.

After MRL training, option 3 becomes the right move: keep the first $m$ numbers, re-normalize, and search.

Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

blocks.question: Your team stores 768-d vectors from a model trained the usual way, with no Matryoshka loss. To save memory, someone proposes keeping only the first 128 numbers of each stored vector. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Quality matches a 128-d model, because any 128 coordinates carry 1/6 of the information evenly
Quality drops more than a model trained at 128 dims would, because the model never learned to put key information first
Quality is unchanged, because cosine similarity is scale invariant
The vectors become invalid and cosine similarity cannot be computed
blocks.explain: A normally trained model spreads information across all coordinates, so a prefix is close to a random subset (Table 2's first-m-dims baseline). It still computes, and cosine still works, but it loses more than a model trained for that size. Scale invariance is about vector length, not about which coordinates you dropped.

lessons.title: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector

blocks.md:
Truncation itself is one line: keep the first $m$ numbers. The subtle part is length. Embeddings are usually stored at unit length, so a dot product equals cosine similarity. Once you cut coordinates off, the prefix is shorter than 1, and each document loses a *different* amount of length.

Toy example: an 8-number unit vector $v$ (simplified; real models use 256 to 3072 numbers). We cut it to 4, then to 2.

blocks.title: Truncating an 8-d unit vector and re-normalizing

scenes.caption: The full vector has length 1: the squares of its 8 entries sum to 1.
Keep the first m = 4 entries. Their length is only 0.871, because the dropped entries held part of the length.
Divide each kept entry by 0.871. The prefix now has length 1 again and points in the same direction.
Cut to m = 2: the prefix length is 0.745, so dividing gives 0.834 and -0.551. Each size needs its own re-normalization.

blocks.caption: Truncate to the first m coordinates, then divide by the prefix length. Numbers from the toy vector above.

blocks.md: Does skipping this step matter? Take the toy $v$ as a query and two documents $X$ and $Y$, both unit length at 8 dims. $X$ has a long prefix that points somewhat away from the query. $Y$ has a short prefix that points almost exactly along it. Over all 8 dims, $Y$ is the better match.

blocks.prompt: At m = 4, you compare the query with each document using a plain dot product of the truncated, un-normalized vectors. Which document ranks first?
blocks.reveal:
**$X$ wins, 0.635 to 0.447, which is the wrong answer.** A raw dot product is cosine times both lengths. $X$'s prefix keeps length 0.903 while $Y$'s keeps only 0.515, and that length gap outweighs the angle.

True cosine on the prefixes divides out the lengths: $Y$ scores 0.997 and $X$ 0.808, matching the full-vector order ($Y$ 0.868, $X$ 0.525).

blocks.title: Scores for documents X and Y under three scoring rules

scenes.caption: Full 8-d cosine: Y is the better match (0.868 vs 0.525).
Raw dot of the 4-d prefixes, no re-normalization: X jumps ahead (0.635 vs 0.447) only because its prefix is longer.
Normalizing only the query divides both scores by the same 0.871 (0.730 vs 0.513). The wrong order stays.
Cosine of the 4-d prefixes (both sides re-normalized): Y is first again (0.997 vs 0.808).

blocks.md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def truncate(emb: np.ndarray, m: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """emb: (n, d) array of embeddings. Returns unit-length m-d prefixes."""
    prefix = emb[:, :m]
    return prefix / np.linalg.norm(prefix, axis=1, keepdims=True)

v = np.array([[0.622, -0.411, 0.351, 0.281, -0.221, 0.251, 0.201, -0.301]])
print(truncate(v, 4).round(3))   # [[ 0.714 -0.472  0.403  0.323]]
blocks.caption: Truncate and re-normalize in NumPy. Sentence Transformers does the same internally during Matryoshka training (slice, then L2-normalize).

blocks.md:
Libraries hide this step for you. In Sentence Transformers, pass `truncate_dim` when loading a model and `encode` returns vectors of that size. OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models take a `dimensions` parameter (defaults: 1536 for text-embedding-3-small, 3072 for text-embedding-3-large), and the guide recommends that parameter over cutting vectors yourself.

Some models need an extra step. Nomic's model card for nomic-embed-text-v1.5 applies a layer norm to the full vector, then slices, then L2-normalizes. Follow each model card's recipe.

blocks.question: You truncate stored 1024-d unit vectors to 256 dims and forget to re-normalize them. Queries are truncated and re-normalized. You rank by dot product. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: re-normalizing the query is enough to restore cosine order
All scores shrink by the same factor, so the order is unchanged
Scores now mix angle with each document's prefix length, so documents with long prefixes are favored
Dot products become negative for every document
blocks.explain: Each stored prefix keeps a different share of its length (0.903 for X and 0.515 for Y in the toy). The dot product multiplies cosine by that length, so long-prefix documents get a boost unrelated to relevance. Normalizing only the query scales every score equally and cannot fix it.

lessons.title: Training a Matryoshka model: one loss per prefix, summed

blocks.md: How do you make the first $m$ numbers useful on their own? Train them to be. MRL picks a small set $\mathcal{M}$ of prefix sizes and applies the model's ordinary loss to each prefix, then adds the losses up. In the paper's ResNet50 setup ($d = 2048$), $\mathcal{M} = \{8, 16, 32, \dots, 1024, 2048\}$, halving each time. For BERT-Base and ViT-B/16 ($d = 768$) it is $\{12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384, 768\}$.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of the MRL paper (classification form). F is the encoder, F(x)_{1:m} its first m outputs, W^(m) a separate linear classifier per size, c_m the weight per size (the paper sets every c_m = 1).

blocks.md:
Gradients from every prefix size flow into the same encoder. The first 8 numbers get pushed by all 9 losses, the last 1024 numbers only by the full-size loss. That is what drives the most useful information to the front.

The paper uses only $O(\log d)$ sizes, not all $d$ of them, yet reports that sizes *between* the trained ones also work well (they interpolate). For text embeddings the loss $\mathcal{L}$ is a contrastive loss instead of a classifier. Each prefix of the query and document vectors is normalized and scored on its own.

**Toy run.** A batch of 3 query-document pairs with 8-d vectors: query q1 should match A, q2 match C, q3 match E. The loss is in-batch cross-entropy over cosine scores times 20, which is how Sentence Transformers' MultipleNegativesRankingLoss works by default (scale 20). Each query's correct document competes with the other two. We compute it at prefixes $\mathcal{M} = \{2, 4, 8\}$, first for a model whose front coordinates hold the topic, then for a standard model.

blocks.title: Cosine scores in the batch at each prefix size

scenes.caption: Matryoshka-style model, m = 2: dims 1 to 2 hold only the topic. A and C share a topic, so q1 and q2 score both near 1. Loss 0.462, close to ln 2 for two of three rows.
Matryoshka-style model, m = 4: dims 3 to 4 add the subtopic, which separates A from C (0.58). Loss falls to 0.000.
m = 8: the full vectors. The diagonal wins every row. Loss 0.000. Summed over the three sizes: 0.463.
Standard model (same full vectors, information spread across all 8 coordinates), m = 2: q1 prefers C (1.00) over its match A (0.99). Loss 0.490.
Standard model, m = 4: q1 still prefers C. Loss 0.379. Only at m = 8 is it 0.000. Summed: 0.870, nearly double the Matryoshka model.

blocks.title: Loss per prefix size and the summed MRL loss

scenes.caption: Standard model. A full-size-only loss would see 0.000 and stop, but the summed MRL loss is 0.870: the small prefixes are the problem.
Matryoshka-style model: only m = 2 still pays (0.462), because 2 numbers cannot hold the subtopic. Sum 0.463. Gradient descent on the sum moves the standard model toward this layout.

blocks.md: Simplified: the toy vectors are hand-built, and the standard model is the Matryoshka one rotated by a fixed random orthogonal matrix. Rotation keeps every full 8-d cosine identical but spreads information across coordinates, mimicking how normal training diffuses it.

**MRL-E (efficient).** Plain MRL gives each size its own classifier $W^{(m)}$. MRL-E ties them: $W^{(m)} = W_{1:m}$, the first $m$ columns of one shared $W$. The paper says this cuts classifier memory by almost half, which matters for huge label spaces. The cost: on ImageNet-1K linear classification MRL-E stays within 1% of the separately trained models from 16 dims up, but at 8 dims it gets 56.66% top-1 against 66.63% for MRL. Masked language modeling reduces to MRL-E automatically, because BERT already ties its output layer to the input embedding matrix.

blocks.title: Where the nested losses attach (ResNet50, d = 2048)

scenes.caption: One forward pass produces z. Nine prefixes (8, 16, ..., 2048) are sliced from the same vector at no extra encoder cost.
Each prefix feeds its own linear classifier and loss. The nine losses are added with weight 1 each.
Backpropagation: the first 8 coordinates receive gradient from all nine losses, the last 1024 only from the full-size loss.
MRL-E: the classifiers share weights, W(m) = first m columns of one W(2048). Fewer parameters, but lower accuracy at the smallest size (56.66 vs 66.63 at 8 dims).

blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import (
    MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, MatryoshkaLoss)

model = SentenceTransformer("microsoft/mpnet-base")
base = MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)          # in-batch negatives, scale 20
loss = MatryoshkaLoss(model, base,
                      matryoshka_dims=[768, 512, 256, 128, 64])
# matryoshka_weights defaults to 1 for every size.
# n_dims_per_step=k samples k sizes per step to save compute (-1 = all).
blocks.caption: Wrapping an ordinary contrastive loss with MatryoshkaLoss in Sentence Transformers. Internally each size slices the embedding, L2-normalizes it and calls the base loss.

blocks.md: The paper's ablations add two practical notes. Weighting the losses differently can lift the small sizes without hurting the large ones. Very small starting sizes (where accuracy is poor) and evenly spaced sizes work worse than the usual halving schedule. Hugging Face's write-up reports that MatryoshkaLoss adds no notable training time in its experiments.

blocks.question: A team trains with MatryoshkaLoss using matryoshka_dims = [768, 512, 256]. In production they truncate to 64 dims and quality is poor. What is the most likely cause?
options: They forgot that Matryoshka models must be queried at exactly 768 dims
64 is below the smallest trained size, so nothing pushed the first 64 coordinates to work alone
MatryoshkaLoss only works with CoSENTLoss, not contrastive losses
Truncated vectors cannot be compared with cosine similarity
blocks.explain: Prefix sizes between trained sizes tend to interpolate, but nothing in training made a 64-d prefix useful on its own. Include the smallest size you plan to serve in matryoshka_dims. Any base loss works, and cosine works on re-normalized prefixes.

blocks.question: In the toy batch at m = 2, the Matryoshka-style model's loss is about 0.462. Why that value?
options: Two of the three queries score their match and one negative almost equally, giving about ln 2 = 0.693 each; averaged over 3 rows that is 0.462
It is the full-size loss divided by 2 because m = 2
Each row contributes 0.462 because the scale is 20
It is a random number; losses at small prefixes are noise
blocks.explain: With two near-equal scores, softmax puts about half its probability on the correct document, and the cross-entropy is -ln(0.5) = 0.693. q1 and q2 each pay that, q3 pays about 0, so the batch mean is 2 x 0.693 / 3 = 0.462.

lessons.title: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard

blocks.md:
Now a search view of the same toy. One query (q1 from the last lesson) and five documents: **A** is the true best match, **B** has the same topic and subtopic but different details, **C** has the same topic but another subtopic, and **D** and **E** have other topics.

In the Matryoshka-style model, dims 1 to 2 hold the topic, dims 3 to 4 the subtopic, dims 5 to 8 the details. The standard model holds the same full vectors, rotated so that information is spread across all 8 coordinates.

blocks.title: Where the query vector keeps its length

scenes.caption: The same query in both models, each with unit length. Their full 8-d cosine with every document is identical. Entries are rounded to 2 decimals, so squaring them gives shares that differ slightly.
Cumulative share of squared length kept by the first m coordinates. The Matryoshka query keeps 66.5% in 2 numbers and 88.2% in 4.
The standard query keeps only 9.6% in its first 2 numbers and 9.7% in 4. Most of it sits in coordinate 6, where a prefix never looks.

blocks.prompt: Rank the five documents by cosine using only the first 2 coordinates. Which document do you expect at the top for each model?
blocks.reveal:
Matryoshka model: **B, A, C** are nearly tied at the top (1.000, 1.000, 0.998), and **D, E** fall far behind. Two numbers hold only the topic, so all three same-topic documents look alike, but the ranking is still sensible.

Standard model: **C** comes first (0.9999), ahead of B and A, and the 2-d prefix is a thin, noisy slice of the vector. It ranks a wrong-subtopic document first.

blocks.title: Cosine of q1 with each document at m = 2, 4, 8

scenes.caption: Matryoshka, m = 2: same-topic A, B, C all near 1.0. D at 0.239, E negative (-0.120; bar height shows size). Order: B, A, C, D, E.
Matryoshka, m = 4: the subtopic separates C (0.577). A and B are still tied (0.998) because they differ only in dims 5 to 8.
Matryoshka, m = 8: details split A (0.997) from B (0.757). Order A, B, C, D, E. Each step only refined the order.
Standard, m = 2: C ranks first (1.000) and A third (0.989). D and E look strongly negative (-0.680, -0.580).
Standard, m = 4: C is still first (0.990), then A (0.983); B drops to 0.668.
Standard, m = 8: identical to the Matryoshka scores, by construction. Both models agree at full size and differ only in their prefixes.

blocks.md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why Matryoshka prefixes are safe for shortlisting.

Real models show the same pattern. On ImageNet-1K nearest-neighbor classification with ResNet50 (paper, Table 2), the MRL model matches a separately trained model at every size and beats it at small sizes. At 8 dims it gets 62.19% against 58.93%; at 2048 dims it is 0.22 points behind (70.97 vs 71.19). Image retrieval (mAP@10) shows MRL up to 3% above the separate models.

For text, Hugging Face trained mpnet-base on AllNLI with and without MatryoshkaLoss and scored both on STS Benchmark. At 64 of 768 dims (8.3% of the size), the Matryoshka model kept 98.37% of its full-size score versus 96.46% for the standard model.

scenes.caption: m = 8: MRL 62.19 beats even the dedicated 8-d model (58.93). MRL-E 57.45. Chopping a normal model: 2.36.
m = 32: MRL 69.46, FF 68.84, MRL-E 68.6. The chopped normal model is at 32.91.
m = 128: MRL 70.52, FF 69.35. The prefix of one MRL model replaces a dedicated model at each size.
m = 2048: all close to 71 (MRL 70.97, FF 71.19). MRL costs almost nothing at full size.

blocks.md: A production example: Nomic's nomic-embed-text-v1.5 model card lists MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) averages of 62.28 at 768 dims, 61.96 at 512, 61.04 at 256, 59.34 at 128 and 56.10 at 64. That is 98.0% of the full score at one third of the size, and 90.1% at one twelfth. Quality loss is gentle at first, then speeds up at the smallest sizes.

blocks.question: With a Matryoshka model you shortlist with 2-d prefixes and keep the top 3 documents. In the toy, which statement is true?
options: The shortlist is B, A, C, so the true best match A survives, and the 8-d rerank puts A first
The shortlist is A, B, C in exact final order, so no rerank is needed
The shortlist is C, B, A, so A is lost
A 2-d prefix cannot be used for search at all
blocks.explain: At m = 2 the Matryoshka scores are B 1.000, A 1.000, C 0.998: the right documents, in blurred order. Reranking those three at m = 8 gives A 0.997, B 0.757, C 0.616. A shortlist needs to contain the right items, not order them perfectly.

lessons.title: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number

blocks.md:
A stored vector costs (number of dims) x (bytes per number). Common precisions:

- **float32**: 4 bytes per number, the usual default.
- **float16**: 2 bytes.
- **int8 (scalar quantization)**: 1 byte. Each dimension's range, learned from a calibration set, is split into 256 buckets.
- **binary**: 1 bit, or 1/8 byte. Each number becomes 1 if it is above 0, else 0, and similarity becomes Hamming distance (the count of differing bits).

Truncation shrinks the first factor and quantization shrinks the second, so the savings multiply.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes per vector} = m \times b, \qquad \text{index size} = N \times m \times b
blocks.caption: m = kept dimensions, b = bytes per number (4, 2, 1 or 1/8), N = number of vectors. Raw vectors only; approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index structures such as HNSW graphs add more.

blocks.title: Bytes per vector by kept dimensions and precision

scenes.caption: Full size, full precision: 12,288 bytes for a 3072-d float32 vector (text-embedding-3-large default size).
Truncating 3072 to 256 dims divides by 12: 1,024 bytes. Same model, one parameter changed.
Quantizing alone: binary at full size is 384 bytes, 32x smaller than float32.
Both: 256-d binary is 32 bytes, 384x smaller than 12,288. 1024-d float32 to 128-d binary is 4096 to 16 bytes, 256x.

blocks.title: Raw vector memory for N vectors

scenes.caption: m = 1024: 10M float32 vectors take 40.96 GB, int8 10.24 GB, binary 1.28 GB.
m = 3072 (full text-embedding-3-large): 10M float32 vectors need 122.88 GB.
m = 256: 10M float32 vectors fit in 10.24 GB, and binary in 0.32 GB. Drag m to explore.

blocks.md:
Hugging Face's embedding quantization post gives a real-scale check: 250 million 1024-d vectors take about 953.67 GB in float32, 238.41 GB in int8 and 29.80 GB in binary (its GB are 2^30 bytes; in the 10^9-byte GB used above, float32 is 1,024 GB). Measured on MTEB retrieval with mxbai-embed-large-v1, binary search kept about 92.5% of retrieval quality, rising to about 96% when a float32 query rescored the binary results (fetching a larger shortlist added nothing more). int8 with rescoring kept about 99%.

That post calls quantization independent of Matryoshka truncation and suggests combining them, for example 1024 to 128 dims and then binary. Its gains for the combination are labeled as the authors' suspicion, not measured.

Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

blocks.question: You store 10M vectors from text-embedding-3-large. Option 1: 3072-d float32. Option 2: 1024-d int8. How much smaller is option 2?
options: 3x
4x
blocks.explain: Option 1: 3072 x 4 = 12,288 bytes per vector (122.88 GB). Option 2: 1024 x 1 = 1,024 bytes (10.24 GB). The ratio is 3 (dims) x 4 (bytes) = 12.

blocks.question: Binary quantization sets each number to 1 if it is above 0. Why does this pair naturally with a shortlist-then-rescore design?
options: Binary vectors are exact, so rescoring is only for logging
Hamming distance on bits is very cheap but coarse, so it finds candidates fast and a higher-precision score fixes their order
Rescoring converts the bits back into the original float values
Binary vectors cannot be searched; they are only for storage
blocks.explain: One bit per dimension makes comparison very cheap but loses magnitude information. The HF post retrieves a larger binary shortlist, then rescores it with the float32 query, recovering much of the lost quality. The bits cannot be turned back into the original floats.

lessons.title: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search

blocks.md:
Lesson 4 showed that a Matryoshka prefix gives a blurred but correct ranking. **Adaptive retrieval** uses that: shortlist $K$ candidates from the whole corpus with a small prefix of size $D_s$, then rerank only those $K$ with a larger prefix $D_r$. Both come from the *same* stored vector, so there is no second model and no second encoding pass.

Cost with exact search, counting multiply-adds per query: one scan of all $N$ vectors at $D_s$ dims, plus $K$ comparisons at $D_r$ dims.

blocks.tex: \text{cost} = D_s \cdot N + K \cdot D_r \quad\text{vs.}\quad d \cdot N \text{ for single-shot search}
blocks.caption: With N = 1,281,167 (ImageNet-1K training set), single-shot at 2048 dims costs about 2.62 GFLOPs. D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048 costs 20.5M + 0.41M = 20.9 MFLOPs, about 125x less.

blocks.md: The paper ran exactly this on ImageNet-1K image retrieval: $D_s = 16$, $K = 200$, $D_r = 2048$ matched single-shot 2048-d accuracy while being about 128x cheaper in theory and about 14x faster in wall-clock time (with HNSW on the same hardware). Reranking 200 vectors at 2048 dims is only 0.41M multiply-adds; the shortlist scan dominates. On the harder ImageNet-4K it needed $D_s = 64$, for about 32x theoretical and 6x real speedups.

blocks.title: Toy shortlist of 2 at m = 2, then rerank at m = 8

scenes.caption: Matryoshka model: the 2-d scan ranks B, A, C, D, E. Keep the top K = 2: B and A.
Rerank B and A with the full 8 dims: A 0.997, B 0.757. A is first, the right answer.
Standard model: the 2-d scan ranks C, B, A, E, D. The top 2 are C and B; A is cut.
Reranking cannot recover a document the shortlist dropped: the result is B (0.757), then C (0.616). Recall of the first stage limits the whole pipeline.

blocks.md: Choosing $D_s$ and $D_r$ is fiddly, so the paper also proposes **funnel retrieval**: rerank several times, halving the shortlist and doubling the prefix at each step. On ImageNet-1K, shortlists of 200, 100, 50, 25, 10 with prefixes 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 2048 matched single-shot 2048-d accuracy at about 128x lower theoretical cost.

blocks.title: Funnel retrieval on ImageNet-1K (cost per query)

scenes.caption: Baseline: comparing the query with all 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims costs about 2.62 billion multiply-adds.
Funnel step 1 scans everything, but at 16 dims: 20.5M multiply-adds. This is the only step that touches the whole corpus.
Each rerank step halves the list and doubles the dims, so steps 2 to 5 cost 6,400 each (200 x 32, 100 x 64, ...).
The last step orders 10 items at full 2048 dims (20,480). Total 20.54M, about 128x below single-shot. Simplified: exact search; real systems use ANN for step 1.

blocks.md:
**In real text-search systems** the pattern looks like this:

- Index small, rerank big. Build the ANN index (for example HNSW) over short or binary-quantized prefixes, keep full or int8 vectors on disk or in a cheaper tier, and rescore a shortlist a few times larger than the final top-k.
- Encode once. Store the full vector and derive every prefix from it; changing the serving size later needs no re-encoding.
- Keep sizes consistent. Query and documents must use the same prefix length and re-normalization, and every prefix size needs its own index.
- Not every model can be truncated. Only models trained for it (text-embedding-3 via its `dimensions` parameter, nomic-embed-text-v1.5, models trained with MatryoshkaLoss) promise usable prefixes.
The first stage must have high recall and the last stage high precision. Matryoshka prefixes give a cheap high-recall first stage from the same vector the precise stage uses.

blocks.question: In a shortlist-then-rerank system with a Matryoshka model, recall@10 is too low. Shortlist K = 50 at D_s = 64, rerank at 1024. Which change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Rerank with 2048 dims instead of 1024
Store the full vectors in float64 for the rerank stage
Enlarge the shortlist (larger K) or use a larger D_s, so the right documents survive the first stage
Normalize only the query vectors
blocks.explain: Reranking can only reorder what the shortlist found. If relevant documents are cut in stage 1, a better stage 2 cannot bring them back. Raising K or D_s increases first-stage recall. Normalizing only the query does not change any order.

blocks.question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
blocks.explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.
